text: Of the 36 plays in Shakespeare's First Folio (1623), 18 had never been printed before, including Macbeth, The Tempest and Twelfth Night. Without his fellow actors Heminges and Condell, they might have been lost.

Apart from six signatures, none spelled "Shakespeare", the only handwriting that may be his is three pages of the play Sir Thomas More, in a hand scholars call Hand D. Many, but not all, accept them as his.

"Elementary, my dear Watson" never appears in Conan Doyle's 60 Sherlock Holmes stories. Holmes says "Elementary" and "my dear Watson", but never together; the full line grew up in stage and later adaptations.

There is no evidence Hemingway wrote the six-word story "For sale: baby shoes, never worn." Similar newspaper items go back to 1906, and the Hemingway attribution surfaces only decades after his death.

In June 1816, during the "Year Without a Summer" that followed the eruption of Tambora, Lord Byron challenged his guests at the Villa Diodati near Geneva to write ghost stories. Mary Shelley, 18, began Frankenstein.

In 1614 an author calling himself Avellaneda published a fake sequel to Don Quixote. In Cervantes's real Part II (1615), characters discuss the impostor's book, and Don Quixote changes his travel plans to prove it wrong.
Georges Perec's novel La Disparition (1969) runs to about 300 pages without once using the letter e. Gilbert Adair's English translation, A Void (1994), keeps the same rule.
The critic Wayne C. Booth coined the term "unreliable narrator" in The Rhetoric of Fiction (1961), for narrators whose account the reader gradually learns not to trust.

In Morphology of the Folktale (1928), Vladimir Propp analyzed 100 Russian fairy tales and argued that all of them are built from just 31 recurring plot functions, which always occur in the same order.

In 1872 George Smith, a self-taught Assyriologist at the British Museum, read a flood story on a clay tablet of the Epic of Gilgamesh. By E. A. Wallis Budge's later account, he got so excited he began to undress.
At about 1.8 million words, the Mahabharata is roughly ten times as long as the Iliad and the Odyssey combined. Its longest version runs to over 100,000 verses.
Sappho probably composed around 10,000 lines of poetry; about 650 survive, and only one poem, the Ode to Aphrodite, is complete. New papyri still turn up, including poems identified in 2004 and 2014.

Beowulf survives in a single manuscript, the Nowell Codex. In 1731 it was scorched in a fire in the Cotton library, and its burned edges kept crumbling for over a century before anyone repaired them properly.
Dante called his poem simply the Comedìa. Boccaccio praised it as "divine", and the title Divina Commedia first appeared on a Venice edition in 1555, more than 230 years after Dante's death.

John Keats, dying of tuberculosis at 25, asked that his gravestone carry no name. The stone in Rome's Protestant Cemetery calls him only "a young English poet" and reads: "Here lies One Whose Name was writ in Water."

Coleridge claimed Kubla Khan came to him in a dream, and that he was writing it down when "a person on business from Porlock" called. When he got back to it an hour later, the rest of the poem was gone.
Flaubert probably never said "Madame Bovary, c'est moi." It appears in none of his works or letters; the scholar Yvan Leclerc traced it to hearsay first printed in 1909, 29 years after Flaubert died.

Under a contract letting a publisher print his works free for nine years if he missed a deadline, Dostoevsky dictated The Gambler in under a month in 1866 to a stenographer, Anna Snitkina. They married the next year.

Mikhail Bulgakov burned his first draft of The Master and Margarita in 1930. The novel, in which the devil insists that "manuscripts don't burn", reached print only in 1966 to 1967, censored, 26 years after his death.

James Joyce set all of Ulysses on a single day, June 16, 1904, the date of his first outing with Nora Barnacle, the woman he later married. Readers around the world now celebrate it every year as Bloomsday.
Ezra Pound cut T. S. Eliot's draft of The Waste Land so heavily that Eliot dedicated the poem to him as "il miglior fabbro", "the better craftsman", a phrase borrowed from Dante's Purgatorio.
For the 1915 first edition of The Metamorphosis, Kafka told his publisher: "The insect itself is not to be drawn. It is not even to be seen from a distance." The cover shows a man in despair instead.
Chinua Achebe took the title of Things Fall Apart (1958) from a line in W. B. Yeats's poem "The Second Coming". The novel answered European fiction about Africa with Igbo life seen from the inside.

Held without trial in Kenya's Kamiti Maximum Security Prison in 1978, Ngũgĩ wa Thiong'o wrote Caitaani Mũtharaba-Inĩ (Devil on the Cross) on prison toilet paper. It is called the first modern novel in Gikuyu.
"The epoch of world literature is at hand, and everyone must strive to hasten its approach." (Johann Wolfgang von Goethe, Conversations with Eckermann, 1827)

Aladdin and Ali Baba appear in no known Arabic manuscript of the Thousand and One Nights. Antoine Galland added them to his French version after hearing them in Paris in 1709 from Hanna Diyab, a storyteller from Aleppo.
"[Beckett] has written a play in which nothing happens, twice." (Vivian Mercier, review of Waiting for Godot, The Irish Times, 1956)

In Borges's story "Pierre Menard, Author of the Quixote" (1939), a modern writer produces chapters word-for-word identical to Cervantes, and the narrator judges them richer and subtler than the original.
In "The Intentional Fallacy" (1946), W. K. Wimsatt and Monroe Beardsley argued that an author's intention is neither available nor a fit standard for judging a poem; the text itself is the evidence.

Kabuki began around 1603, when a woman named Izumo no Okuni staged dances on a dry riverbed in Kyoto. In 1629 the shogunate banned women from the kabuki stage, and male actors took over the female roles.
